extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students in mathematical logic and computability theory; readers learning representability of computable functions in first-order arithmetic (theory Q)
extracted.subtask_description: Show which functions and relations are representable in Robinson arithmetic Q, give explicit representations for basic functions, simulate primitive recursion with composition+regular minimization (via the β-function), and derive consequences (undecidability, Σ1-completeness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing function definable without primitive recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: The pairing function, J(x, y) = 1 2 [(x + y)(x + y + 1)] + x, is definable using 0, successor, plus, times, χ=, projections, composition and minimization applied to regular functions (i.e., without primitive recursion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as item (1) of functions definable without primitive recursion; used to encode pairs and hence sequences. The textbook uses this pairing function (Cantor pairing) to code pairs into single natural numbers for further constructions (e.g., coding d = J(d0,d1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection functions definable without primitive recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: Projection functions K(z) = (min x ≤ z) (∃y ≤ z) z = J(x, y) and L(z) = (min y ≤ z) (∃x ≤ z) z = J(x, y) are definable without primitive recursion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These functions recover the first and second components of an encoded pair z via bounded minimization and bounded quantification; they are necessary for decoding codes like d = J(d0,d1) in later constructions (e.g., β(d,i) = β*(K(d),L(d),i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Less-than relation definable without primitive recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation x < y can be defined using only the permitted basic functions/operations and bounded quantification / minimization (so it does not require primitive recursion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (3) in the list of definable things; the text relies on definability of < for many Q-provability lemmas (e.g., bounded quantifier manipulations, lemmas about x<0 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility relation definable without primitive recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: The divisibility relation x | y is definable from the basic functions and bounded quantification/minimization (no primitive recursion needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (4) in the enumerated definable relations; used earlier when constructing relatively prime numbers and in the β-function lemma argument where primality/divisibility properties are invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remainder function rem(x,y) definable without primitive recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: The function rem(x, y), returning the remainder when y is divided by x, is definable without primitive recursion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item (5) in the list of definable things; rem is used to define β*(d0,d1,i) = rem(1 + (i + 1)d1, d0), which recovers sequence elements via congruences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of β* and β (β-function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define β*(d0, d1, i) = rem(1 + (i + 1)d1, d0) and β(d, i) = β*(K(d), L(d), i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This β is the standard β-function used to code finite sequences into a single number d = J(d0,d1); K and L recover d0 and d1. The construction depends on definability of rem and the pairing/projection functions. The β-function will be shown to reproduce any finite list a0,...,an as β(d,i)=ai for i≤n for an appropriate d.

rubrics_metrics.name: β-function lemma (existence of code d for a finite sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a finite sequence a0,...,an, there exists a number d such that for each i ≤ n, β(d,i) = ai (β as defined above).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses: pick j = max(n, a0+1, ..., an+1); let d1 = lcm(1,...,j) so 1+(i+1)d1 are pairwise relatively prime and larger than all ai; use Sunzi's Theorem (Chinese Remainder Theorem) to choose d0 with d0 ≡ ai (mod 1+(i+1)d1); set d=J(d0,d1); then β(d,i)=rem(1+(i+1)d1,d0)=ai. This lemma is the key technical tool to encode sequences without primitive recursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation of primitive recursion by composition and regular minimization (Lemma 173A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If h is defined from f and g by primitive recursion (h(⃗x,0)=f(⃗x), h(⃗x,y+1)=g(⃗x,y,h(⃗x,y))), then h can be defined from f, g, zero, succ, projections, add, mult, χ= using composition and regular minimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct auxiliary ˆh(⃗x,y) = µd [β(d,0)=f(⃗x) ∧ (∀i<y) β(d,i+1)=g(⃗x,i,β(d,i))], i.e., the least d coding the initial segment of the recursion; then h(⃗x,y)=β(ˆh(⃗x,y),y). Crucially, this uses only the β-function plus composition and regular minimization (no primitive recursion). The minimized predicate is regular by the β lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal definition/requirements of representability (functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A k-ary function f is represented in a theory (like Q) by a formula αf(x0,...,xk−1,y) iff whenever f(n0,...,nk−1)=m the theory proves αf(n0,...,nk−1,m), and the theory proves ∀y(αf(n0,...,nk−1,y) → y = m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: showing for each basic or constructed function that Q proves the witness sentence and proves uniqueness; this is the standard representability criterion used to show compositional and minimization closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic functions are representable in Q
rubrics_metrics.description: Zero, successor, projections, the characteristic function χ= of equality, addition, and multiplication are representable in Q by simple formulas: αzero(x,y) ≡ y = 0; αsucc(x,y) ≡ y = x′; αP^n_i(...) ≡ y = xi; αχ=(x0,x1,y) ≡ (x0 = x1 ∧ y = 1) ∨ (x0 ≠ x1 ∧ y = 0); αadd(x0,x1,y) ≡ y = (x0 + x1); αmult(x0,x1,y) ≡ y = (x0 × x1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each, one must show Q proves the appropriate instance when fed numerals and proves the uniqueness universal sentence ∀y(α(...,y) → y = k). The text gives proofs (or exercises) for these propositions, relying on lemmas (e.g., Q can prove equalities of closed numerals, Q ⊢ (n+m)=n+m, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation is closed under composition (Propositions 175A–175C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If αf represents f and the αgi represent gi, then αh(x0,...,xl−1,z) ≡ ∃y0...yk−1 (αg0(...,y0) ∧ ··· ∧ αgk−1(...,yk−1) ∧ αf(y0,...,yk−1,z)) represents h(x0,...,xl−1) = f(g0(...),...,gk−1(...)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show: (i) if h(n)=m then Q ⊢ αh(n,m) by existentially exhibiting the intermediate y values; (ii) uniqueness: Q ⊢ ∀z (αh(n,z) → z = m) using uniqueness for αg and αf. The same idea scales to arities >1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation is closed under regular minimization (Proposition 176E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If αg(x,z,y) represents a regular function g(x,z) in Q, and f(z) = µx[g(x,z)=0], then αf(z,y) ≡ αg(y,z,0) ∧ ∀w(w < y → ¬αg(w,z,0)) represents f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof must show Q ⊢ αf(n,m) when f(n)=m (witness and no smaller witness) and Q ⊢ ∀y(αf(n,y) → y = m) using lemmas about <, bounded quantifiers, and properties of Q (Lemmas 176A–176D, 1710E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Every computable (general recursive) function is representable in Q (Theorem 177A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the characterization of general recursive functions (built from zero, succ, projections, add, mult, χ= using composition, primitive recursion, and regular minimization) and the previous lemmas (simulate primitive recursion with β, basic functions representable, closure under composition and regular minimization), every computable function is representable in Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence the set of representable functions in Q equals the set of computable functions; the result also applies to many theories extending Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of representability for relations (Definition 178A)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R(x0,...,xk) on N is representable in Q if there is a formula αR(x0,...,xk) such that whenever R(n0,...,nk) is true, Q proves αR(n0,...,nk), and whenever R(n0,...,nk) is false, Q proves ¬αR(n0,...,nk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the analogue for relations of function representability; the text uses this to relate computability of relations with representability (Theorem 178B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: relations are representable in Q iff computable (Theorem 178B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R is representable in Q if and only if it is computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward direction: if represented by αR, then to decide R(n) search for a proof of αR(n) or ¬αR(n); one will be found. Reverse direction: if R computable, then its characteristic function χR is computable and hence representable by αχR(x,y); define αR(x) := αχR(x,1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provability predicate ProvQ and undecidability of Q (Theorem 179A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation ProvQ(y) ⇔ Sent(y) ∧ ∃x Prf_Q(x,y) (y codes a sentence provable in Q) is not recursive; thus Q is undecidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by reduction from the halting problem using Kleene's T predicate (primitive recursive and representable in Q): one shows Q ⊢ ∃y βT(e,n,y) iff φ_e(n)↓, and then argues that a hypothetical decision procedure for ProvQ would solve the halting problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-order logic undecidable (Corollary 179B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If first-order logic were decidable then provability in Q would be decidable (since Q ⊢ α iff ⊢ τ → α where τ is conjunction of axioms), so FO logic is undecidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct corollary of Theorem 179A; included to show broader implications of representability results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic properties of bounded formulas (∆0) and Σ1, Π1 sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A ∆0 wff is built from atomic wffs using only propositional connectives and bounded quantifiers. A Σ1 wff is of the form ∃x β(x) with β ∆0; a Π1 wff is of the form ∀x β(x) with β ∆0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These syntactic classes are used in the Σ1-completeness theorem: if α is a Σ1 sentence true in the standard model B, then Q ⊢ α (Theorem 1710G). Several lemmas (1710C–1710F) establish that Q proves true ∆0 sentences and manipulates bounded quantifiers over closed terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Σ1-completeness of Q (Theorem 1710G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α is a Σ1 sentence which is true in the standard model B, then Q ⊢ α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: true Σ1 sentence ∃x β(x) has some witness n with β(n) true, β being ∆0; by Lemma 1710F Q ⊢ β(n), hence Q ⊢ ∃x β(x). This shows Q proves all true Σ1 sentences, used in arguments about what Q can and cannot prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical lemmas about Q proving equalities/inequalities of closed terms (Lemmas 1710C–1710E, 176A–176D, 174E, 174G, 174I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various lemmas asserting that Q proves identities like t = n for closed term t evaluating to n, that Q proves (n + m) = n + m and (n × m) = n · m, that Q ⊢ ∀x ¬x < 0, ∀x(x < n+1 → x=0 ∨ ... ∨ x=n), and other bounded-quantifier facts about numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lemmas are the foundational provability facts used to show representability of basic functions and the correctness of constructions involving bounded quantifiers, bounded minimization, and uniqueness proofs. They support the main representability and Σ1-completeness theorems and are used in proofs of propositions (e.g., proving uniqueness ∀y(αf(n,y) → y=m)).
